Q: How do HTML landmarks, headings and forms create an accessible document?
A: Semantic HTML gives browsers and assistive technology meaningful structure before scripts run. Use heading levels to reflect hierarchy, landmarks to identify major regions, labels to name controls and real form elements to provide expected interaction. A button activates an action; a link navigates to a resource. Custom attributes cannot repair every incorrect native element choice. Validate that important content and actions remain understandable when styling fails, keyboard input replaces a pointer, or JavaScript has not loaded.
Why: A visible placeholder disappears after typing and may not supply a durable accessible name. A label linked to the input remains available while an error message can be associated separately.
Risk: A visually polished page can still lack names, landmarks or keyboard-operable controls.
Trade: Native semantics reduce custom interaction code and improve predictable behavior.
Try: Complete a form using only a keyboard and inspect its accessible names and error relationships.
worked_case: A visible placeholder disappears after typing and may not supply a durable accessible name. A label linked to the input remains available while an error message can be associated separately.

Q: How do the CSS cascade, box model and layout systems determine the final page?
A: The cascade resolves competing declarations through origin, importance, layers, specificity and order; layout then uses computed sizes and constraints. The box model distinguishes content, padding, border and margin. Flexbox distributes items primarily along one dimension, while grid arranges two-dimensional tracks. A child can overflow when an intrinsic minimum size exceeds the available track, even if the parent appears responsive. Inspect computed styles and container constraints before adding arbitrary fixed widths or hiding overflow.
Why: A code block inside a grid cell may force horizontal page scrolling. Allow the cell to shrink with min-width:0 and keep the code block itself scrollable rather than clipping the text from users.
Risk: Hiding overflow can conceal required content and keyboard focus.
Trade: Flexible layouts need explicit content bounds and representative long-text checks.
Try: Diagnose a long-token overflow at a narrow viewport using computed widths.
worked_case: A code block inside a grid cell may force horizontal page scrolling. Allow the cell to shrink with min-width:0 and keep the code block itself scrollable rather than clipping the text from users.

Q: How do JavaScript closures and event listeners cause stale values or memory retention?
A:
JavaScript closures retain access to variable bindings within their lexical environment at the time of creation. In React, functional components execute on every render pass, creating an entirely new execution context with fresh local variables and props. A closure created inside that render—such as an event handler, setTimeout callback, or an un-cleaned event listener—captures the specific variable bindings of that individual render snapshot.

A ubiquitous production defect is the stale closure bug. For example, if a component sets up a window resize listener or an interval timer inside a useEffect with an empty dependency array ([]), the callback closes over the initial render state. When the timer fires 10 seconds later, it accesses the variable values from render 0, completely blind to subsequent state updates. If the handler attempts to update state using setCount(count + 1), it perpetually increments from 0 to 1, dropping all intermediate state changes. To resolve stale closures, developers must either include all referenced variables in the effect dependency array, utilize functional state updaters (setCount(c => c + 1)), or capture the latest value in a mutable useRef container.

Furthermore, event listeners and closures represent the leading cause of memory leaks in single-page applications. When a component registers a global listener (e.g., window.addEventListener('scroll', handler)) or subscribes to a WebSocket without removing it in the effect cleanup return function, the global window object retains a reference to the handler. Because the handler closes over its component scope, the entire component subtree, its state, and its detached DOM nodes remain anchored in the V8 garbage collector heap root path, permanently preventing garbage collection and causing memory consumption to grow with every user navigation.
Why: Closures capture render-snapshot lexical scopes, causing un-synchronized callbacks to read obsolete state. Unregistered listeners anchor component subtrees to global roots, permanently preventing garbage collection.
Risk: Stale closures cause silent logic regressions and lost state updates, while unremoved event listeners cause multi-megabyte heap memory leaks that crash long-running client sessions.
Trade: useRef provides access to mutable latest values without re-triggering effect setup, but bypasses React rendering lifecycle and must not be read or written during the render phase.
Try: Create a setInterval inside an effect with an empty dependency array referencing a raw state variable; observe count freezing at 1, then convert to a functional updater to observe continuous increments.
worked_case: Navigating between views can install three resize handlers if each mount adds one and cleanup does nothing. All three may run, with older handlers referencing detached view state.

Q: How do promises, async/await and Promise.all handle failure?
A: A promise represents eventual fulfillment or rejection; async/await makes sequencing explicit without removing those failure states. Promise.all rejects when one input rejects but does not automatically cancel the remaining operations. Promise.allSettled observes every outcome when partial results are meaningful. Decide which operations are independent, which share an effect boundary and which must be cancelled after failure. A catch handler should translate or recover from a known error, not silently convert every failure into successful empty data.
Why: Three independent lookups can finish with two successes and one failure. A dashboard may show partial sections with explicit errors, whereas an all-or-nothing checkout cannot treat the same pattern as a successful complete transaction.
Risk: Rejected aggregation does not imply that sibling side effects stopped.
Trade: Parallel work reduces waiting when independent; explicit sequencing preserves real dependencies.
Try: Demonstrate that a sibling operation still runs after Promise.all rejects.
worked_case: Three independent lookups can finish with two successes and one failure. A dashboard may show partial sections with explicit errors, whereas an all-or-nothing checkout cannot treat the same pattern as a successful complete transaction.

Q: How does TypeScript narrowing differ from runtime validation?
A: TypeScript checks source-level assumptions and erases most type information during compilation. Narrowing uses control flow and discriminants to refine possible types inside the checked program. An external JSON response begins as an untrusted value even if a cast tells the compiler otherwise. Validate its shape and semantic fields before constructing trusted state. Use a discriminated union to represent meaningful states such as loading, ready and failed, so impossible combinations are harder to express. The server must still enforce its own contract.
Why: Casting a response to User does not prove that response.name exists. A malformed response can reach rendering unless runtime validation rejects it and produces a visible error state.
Risk: Type assertions can silence the very boundary uncertainty the program needs to handle.
Trade: Static types reduce internal mistakes; runtime parsers guard external representations.
Try: Parse unknown input into a success/error union without using an unchecked cast.
worked_case: Casting a response to User does not prove that response.name exists. A malformed response can reach rendering unless runtime validation rejects it and produces a visible error state.

Q: How do React state, derived values and stable keys prevent inconsistent interfaces?
A:
In React component architecture, maintaining interface consistency requires strict discipline regarding what constitutes primary state versus derived values, and how component identities are preserved across reconciliation cycles. State should represent the absolute minimal set of mutable values necessary to record user interactions and asynchronous data arrivals. A widespread anti-pattern is duplicating state—such as storing raw items in itemsState, and attempting to synchronize a separate filteredItemsState inside a useEffect. This synchronization introduces an intermediate render where filtered items disagree with the filter query, causing UI flickering, race conditions, and inconsistent derived totals. Derived values must be computed directly during render (e.g., const filtered = items.filter(...)), optionally wrapped in useMemo if the calculation is computationally expensive.

React keys serve as immutable identity anchors for the virtual DOM reconciliation algorithm. When mapping collections of elements, React matches existing DOM nodes and component instances between renders using their key attribute. A catastrophic production defect occurs when developers use array indices as keys (key={index}). If a user deletes the first row or sorts a data grid, the items shift index positions: the second item now receives index 0. React concludes that the component identity has not changed; it re-renders the component with new props while preserving the internal local state (such as uncontrolled text inputs, checkbox toggles, or CSS transition states) of the previous entity. Consequently, a user's unsaved draft text or active selection appears attached to a completely different record. Collections must always use stable, unique entity IDs (e.g., UUIDs or database primary keys), and state updates that depend on preceding values must use functional updater callbacks (setCount(prev => prev + 1)) to prevent dropped updates under concurrent batching.
Why: Deriving values during render eliminates desynchronized state bugs, while unique stable keys guarantee that component identity and local input state follow the entity rather than transient array positions.
Risk: Using array index keys causes form inputs, selections, and focus to attach to the wrong data entities when sorting, filtering, or deleting list rows.
Trade: Computing derived values during render keeps state minimal and consistent, but requires profiling and useMemo if the transformation involves thousands of complex items.
Try: Render an editable table keyed by array index versus item UUID. Delete the top row and observe how the uncontrolled input value corrupts when keyed by index but cleanly preserves data when keyed by UUID.
worked_case: Reordering editable rows keyed by array index can make one person's unsaved text appear under another person's name. A stable row identifier associates the local input state with the correct entity.

Q: When is a React effect necessary, and how should it clean up asynchronous work?
A:
In modern React, useEffect is not a generic lifecycle hook or state orchestration mechanism; it is strictly an escape hatch for synchronizing a component with an external system outside React control (such as DOM event listeners, WebSocket connections, timers, external SDKs, or network fetches). Computations that transform data for rendering belong directly in the render body, and actions triggered by direct user intent (such as submitting a form or clicking a button) belong strictly in event handlers, not in effects listening to state changes.

When an effect initiates asynchronous work, it incurs an absolute obligation to clean up that work when dependencies change or the component unmounts. The effect lifecycle executes in two phases: the setup function runs after React commits the component to the DOM, and the cleanup function runs immediately before re-running setup with new dependencies, as well as upon unmount. In asynchronous data fetching, failing to manage cleanup causes severe race conditions. Consider a user quickly toggling between Customer A and Customer B: the request for A is dispatched, followed by B. If network latency delays A so it resolves after B, a naive handler lacking cleanup will overwrite B’s fresh view with A’s stale data.

To prevent this, cleanup must cancel in-flight work and enforce identity boundaries. Wrapping fetch requests in an AbortController (signal: controller.signal) terminates HTTP network streams at the browser transport layer upon unmount or dependency change. However, because cached network responses or microtasks can still resolve synchronously or arrive before abort processes, effects must also maintain a local active flag (let active = true; return () => { active = false; };) or generational token. If active is false when the promise resolves, the completion callback discards the payload, preventing state poisoning and memory leaks.
Why: Effects synchronize components with external systems. Cleanup functions using AbortController and active boolean flags prevent out-of-order network responses from overwriting newer views with stale data.
Risk: Omitting cleanup leads to out-of-order response overwriting, memory leaks from retained subscriptions, and unexpected duplicate listeners under React StrictMode double-mounting.
Trade: AbortController cancels network transport immediately to save bandwidth, but requires catching and ignoring AbortError in fetch promise chains to prevent spurious error toasts.
Try: Simulate two sequential asynchronous fetches with artificial delays (Request 1 taking 500ms, Request 2 taking 100ms) with and without active cleanup flags to demonstrate race condition resolution.
worked_case: A user changes from account A to B while A's response is delayed. The UI must not render A's result under B even if abort arrives too late to stop A's completion.

Q: How do frontend tests distinguish visual appearance from usable behavior?
A: A screenshot records pixels for one state and viewport; it does not prove keyboard operation, correct accessible names, race handling or safe rendering of hostile text. Test the user-visible contract through real interactions where practical. Include loading, empty, error, cancellation and stale-response states, not only a successful populated view. Automated accessibility tools catch a useful subset of issues, while manual keyboard and assistive-technology review answer different questions. Keep assertions on meaningful outcomes rather than component internals.
Why: A button may look enabled in a screenshot but be unreachable by keyboard or trigger the action twice. A browser interaction can verify focus, activation, disabled state and one accepted operation.
Risk: Passing visual snapshots can coexist with inaccessible or incorrect interactions.
Trade: Choose targeted behavioral checks and visual review according to the failure being prevented.
Try: Test submission using a keyboard and simulate a slow response followed by navigation.
worked_case: A button may look enabled in a screenshot but be unreachable by keyboard or trigger the action twice. A browser interaction can verify focus, activation, disabled state and one accepted operation.
